new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Bari has an empty rule (documentation-ingest, tonal per Yokwe 1987) and its domain quote already cites Owen 1908 secs. 16-17 for the word-accent vs sentence-accent split, so nothing here contradicts it. Owen adds detail the catalog does not carry: no fixed position, imperative oxytone-sg/paroxytone-pl rule, accent kept on the same syllable across tenses, reduplicant accent, enclitic sentence-accent. Read here from the full MPG PuRe PDF rather than the Rosetta excerpt the catalog cites.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Owen gives no fixed position. His 'accent' (acute mark on a short vowel 'read or spoken in a very pronounced manner') is distributed lexically: one class of words has every syllable equally accented (dédé, fáfárásák; the marks are then omitted), another class has one especially prominent syllable, which can be final (agí, adá, lunjí, biú), initial (lóbut, nábut) or penultimate (musála). One morphological generalization: imperatives are oxytone in the singular and paroxytone in the plural (durjyö, plur. durjyöta; sec. 16 Note 1). Verbs (sec. 40, p. 21-22): 'many verbs' have the same accent on each syllable (togorja, milö), others one accented syllable (toyúkan, tuán, tö'ngun); 'The accent of the present must be kept on the same syllable in the perfect and future' (exception tuán, aorist átuan, future tuátuan); 'An unaccented verb takes sometimes by reduplication an accent, and this may also fall on the reduplicative syllable' (meddya, mémeddya). Sec. 17 (p. 6): 'The sentence-accent resembles the enclitica in Greek' — a short word after an oxytone (incl. articles lo/na/ti, prepositions i/ko/ku) is read as an enclitic (dongé lo -> dongélo; ti nan -> tínan). Owen never uses the word tone; the pattern he describes (all syllables of a word 'accented', accent stable across tense forms, accent on a reduplicant) is what a two-tone language looks like when written with an acute for high tone, which is how later work (Yokwe 1987, already in the catalog) treats Bari.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; sec. 16(1) instead allows several equally 'accented' syllables in one word (dédé, fáfárásák).
new_statements.exceptions: Imperatives: oxytone sg. / paroxytone pl. (sec. 16 Note 1); vowel after an accented syllable read 'very short' (Note 2, p. 6); verb tuán shifts accent in aorist/future (sec. 40 exception); 'If stress is laid upon the pronoun, it must take the accent' (sec. 17 Note 2, p. 6: ko dó 'with thee', ko tá nan tutu?).
new_statements.identity_note: Owen 1908 describes the Bari of Mongalla Province, Southern Sudan (Owen was its Governor); the preface places the tribe between roughly 3°40'N and 5°45'N along the Bahr el Jebel, southern boundary the River Assua; no dialect is named. The Spagnolo excerpts carry no dialect information. Glottolog lists Nile Bari, Ligo, Pöjulu, Nyepu, Nyangbara as dialects under bari1284.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog codes Bari 'tonal' on Yokwe 1987, who quotes Spagnolo 1933:9 second-hand; the sec. 15 snippet now confirms that quotation first-hand (agrees) and sec. 83 adds a stress statement the catalog lacks: syllable stress that varies lexically across nouns (final syllable stressed or not) and conditions stressed/unstressed suffix allomorphy, with no three unstressed syllables in a row (refines). This is compatible with the existing Owen 1908-based statement filed as 'lexical (unpredictable)' and with Tucker & Bryan 1966's 'significant shifting of stress in certain circumstances' in Bari; it does not support any fixed-position coding. Snippet-level evidence; pages unverified.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Spagnolo states that Bari is a tone language (every syllable would need a tone mark; he marks only high tone where ambiguity would arise) and, separately, treats stress as a property of individual syllables that differs from noun to noun: some nouns have a stressed final syllable, others an unstressed one, and the singular(ive) suffix is chosen to alternate with it (stressed suffixes -tat/-tot/-töt/-nit after an unstressed final syllable, unstressed -ti/-te/-it/-et/-tyo after a stressed one), with the rhythmic constraint that three unstressed syllables never occur in a row. No fixed stress position is stated in the visible text; stress placement is lexical per noun with rhythmic alternation in suffixation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing explicit; the 'no three unstressed syllables together' constraint implies rhythmic alternation but no secondary-stress statement is visible in the snippets.
new_statements.exceptions: sec. 123: in emphatic speech 'accent on each of the last two syllables of the Adjective, pause between syllables, gives an air of great [..] impressiveness' (expressive, not lexical stress); sec. 105: relative particle + monosyllabic adjective stem 'involve a change in intonation' (tone, sg vs pl).
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe Bari proper (Bari of the Rejaf/Juba area, South Sudan; Spagnolo's mission Bari; Tucker & Bryan's BARI as head of the Bari-Lotuho cluster within 'Paranilotic', with Kakwa, Kuku, Mandari etc. treated as Bari dialects/cluster members).

readall_conflicts: No source opened here states a word-stress placement or contradicts another. The only tension is terminological: Owen 1908 speaks of an 'accent' (acute mark, one or several per word, lexically distributed, stable across verb tenses, oxytone/paroxytone imperatives) and never mentions tone, whereas the catalog's own quote (Yokwe 1987, citing Spagnolo 1933:9 and Tucker & Bryan 1966) describes Bari as a tone language whose tone distinguishes lexical items and marks morphology. Owen's description is consistent with high tone written as an acute, not with a positional stress rule; taken at face value it would be 'lexical (unpredictable)' accent. Tucker & Bryan 1966 (lending-only) and the Spagnolo phonology pages (not in any open copy) could not be read, so whether either says anything about stress as distinct from tone remains unchecked. No contradiction with the catalog's 'tonal' coding. The only new content is snippet-level: Tucker & Bryan 1966 ch. 31 sec. 2b says stress 'falls normally on the Stem syllable of words' in the Paranilotic group and that 'in BARI there is significant shifting of stress in certain circumstances' (tone-class-conditioned examples not recoverable). That characterisation (predictable stem stress with conditioned shift, alongside lexical/grammatical tone) differs from the existing Owen 1908-based statement filed as 'lexical (unpredictable)', but Owen's 'word-accents' (acute on every vowel of certain words) are better understood as tone/vowel marking than…
